title: The Song of the Rescued
summary: Isaiah gives the words the rescued people will sing on the day God's anger turns away and his comfort comes. First a single voice thanks God for becoming its salvation; then the whole community is told to draw joy from the springs of salvation and to make God's name known among the nations. The song ends with a call to Zion to shout for joy, because the Holy One of Israel is great in its midst.
story: Chapters 1 to 12 form the first large movement of Isaiah. They open with a courtroom accusation against Judah, pass through the prophet's call (chapter 6), the crisis of King Ahaz and the sign of Immanuel (chapters 7 and 8), the promised child and the fall of Assyria (chapters 9 and 10), and the vision of the Spirit-filled king and the gathering of the exiles (chapter 11). Chapter 12 closes the movement with worship. After so much judgment, the section ends not with a warning but with a hymn. The next section, beginning in chapter 13, turns to the nations, and this song has already prepared for it by telling Zion to make God's deeds known “among the peoples” and “in all the earth.”
historical:
The chapter itself names no king or event, since it looks forward to “that day”, the time of rescue described in chapter 11. It belongs to the world of Isaiah's ministry in Jerusalem in the late eighth century BC, when Judah lived under the shadow of Assyria and had watched the northern kingdom of Israel fall in 722 BC. Some scholars think this closing hymn was added when the book's first section was being arranged, perhaps later than Isaiah himself, because it gathers phrases from the Psalms and from Exodus in the way worship songs often do. Others see no reason it could not come from the prophet, who elsewhere writes psalm-like poetry. Either way, it was placed deliberately to round off chapters 1 to 11.

The song borrows its central line from Israel's oldest story of rescue. When Israel crossed the sea out of Egypt, Moses and the people sang that the LORD was their strength and song and had become their salvation (Exodus 15:2). Isaiah 11 had just promised a second exodus with a highway home; chapter 12 gives the people the second exodus song.
cultural:
Water in the dry hill country of Judah was never taken for granted. Jerusalem depended on the Gihon spring outside its walls and on cisterns carved into the rock to catch the winter rain. Drawing water was daily work, usually done by women and girls at a spring or well, and a reliable spring meant life for a town. To speak of drawing water “from the springs of salvation” turns an ordinary chore into a picture of joy that never runs dry.

Later Jewish practice gave verse 3 a festival setting. During the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot, the autumn harvest festival when Israel lived in booths to remember the wilderness years), priests in the Second Temple period drew water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, and rabbinic writings associate the joy of that ceremony with this verse. The hymn's calls to praise, proclaim, and sing are the vocabulary of temple worship, where the congregation gave thanks aloud and told of God's deeds.
literary: The chapter is a short hymn in two stanzas, each introduced by “you will say” (verses 1 and 4). In the first the “you” is singular: one worshiper speaks of God's anger turning away and of comfort, trust, and salvation. Verse 3 is a bridge in the plural. In the second stanza the address is to the whole people, and the praise turns outward: make his works known, declare his name, let this be known in all the earth. The word salvation appears three times in verses 2 and 3, holding the song together, and the final line gathers the book's favorite title for God, “the Holy One of Israel,” first heard in Isaiah 1:4.

outline.t: A personal song: God's anger turned to comfort, God my salvation
Drawing water with joy from the springs of salvation
A community song: make his name known among the nations
Zion's shout: the Holy One of Israel is great among you

doctrines.note: Salvation here is God's own act and God's own presence: “God is my salvation.” The song does not thank God for providing a way out; it says he has become the rescue itself.
Rescued Israel is not to keep the news to itself. The second stanza sends God's praise outward to the peoples and to all the earth, so that worship and witness belong together.

The Holy One of Israel, whose holiness terrified Isaiah in chapter 6, is now great in the midst of his people as the reason for their joy. The holy God who judged sin is the same God who dwells with the forgiven.

words.note: Yeshuah, salvation, rescue, or deliverance. It appears three times in verses 2 and 3 and usually means concrete rescue from enemies or danger rather than an inner state. It is closely related to the names Joshua and Isaiah, both of which mean something like the LORD saves, and to the Aramaic form of Jesus's name, Yeshua.

Nacham, here to comfort. The same verb can mean to be sorry or to relent, but in verse 1 it describes God consoling the one he had been angry with. It anticipates the famous opening of Isaiah 40, “Comfort, comfort My people,” where the same root carries the book's turn toward hope.

Yadah, to give thanks or praise, often by publicly acknowledging what someone has done. It opens both stanzas (verses 1 and 4). Thanksgiving in Israel was a spoken confession before others, which is why it leads naturally into telling the nations.

christ: The link between this chapter and Jesus is partly verbal and partly thematic. On the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the festival whose water ceremony later tradition tied to verse 3, Jesus stood and invited anyone who was thirsty to come to him and drink, promising rivers of living water (John 7:37-38). John does not quote Isaiah 12 there, but the setting makes the echo hard to miss. More broadly, the song celebrates God himself becoming salvation, and Christians confess that in Jesus, whose name means the LORD saves, God did exactly that. The move from one rescued voice to a message for all the peoples also anticipates the church's calling to make God's deeds known among the nations.
questions: Verse 1 speaks honestly of God's anger before it speaks of comfort. Why might it matter that the song remembers the anger rather than skipping it?
The first stanza is personal and the second is public. How does gratitude for what God has done for you turn into telling others?
What would it look like in an ordinary week to draw water with joy from the springs of salvation?
